<description>
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.
</description>

[2026-10-27] r:5667388831 review COMMENTED by musaHaruna (contributor):
I've spent some time going through the discussion in[ #33510](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33510) and the history of mempool expiry. I agree that removing transactions simply because they've been in the mempool for 14 days isn't ideal, especially when an old parent could become attractive through a new high-fee child.

My main concern with removing expiry entirely is the possibility of retaining high-feerate transactions that miners won't include, for example when an outdated node accepts transactions that violate newer policies adopted by miners, such as[ #32521](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32521). `TrimToSize()` wouldn't necessarily help here, since those transactions are still highly ranked locally. Under memory pressure, they could displace lower-feerate transactions that miners would actually include, potentially causing more `SIZELIMIT` removals and raising the minimum mempool feerate.

I agree with **stickies-v** that this mostly concerns outdated nodes, and expiry isn't particularly effective against an attacker who keeps rebroadcasting. However, it does provide eventual recovery from a one-time attack or persistent policy disagreement when the transactions are no longer being submitted.

The data shared by **0xB10C** shows that expiry removes transactions that can later be mined, but I'm not sure it tells us enough about the tradeoff. How often does expiry remove economically attractive transactions or CPFP packages, compared with how often it actually frees capacity occupied by transactions miners won't include? And would removing it lead to more size-based evictions or a higher minimum mempool feerates under pressure?

Looking at the hybrid approach suggested by **Ismaelsadeeq**, i.e combining transaction age with missed mining opportunities, possibly only under memory pressure. I'm leaning toward exploring this longer term, but it has its own problems. Local template inclusion doesn't establish that miners received or rejected a transaction, and counting missed opportunities could penalize censored transactions. There are also the costs of template construction and the question of what happens to previous observations when a parent receives a new high-fee child.

There's also the interaction with fee estimation following[ #34075](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34075). Persistently unmined, high-feerate transactions could affect the mempool-based estimator despite its health checks. But I think that such transactions for estimation don't require removing them from the mempool. I think this is worth investigating separately, rather than using fee estimation as a reason to retain expiry.

Given this, I'm leaning toward deprecating `-mempoolexpiry` rather than removing its functionality immediately, with age expiry disabled by default but still available explicitly during the deprecation period. This would preserve a recovery option for operators while giving us a chance to understand the consequences of the changed default.

Finally, Is there already evidence that the protection expiry provides against persistent policy disagreement is negligible enough to justify removing the mechanism entirely, rather than just changing the default?

I'd appreciate corrections in case I missed something.
</new_statements>
